title: Parts Shop Showdown
covers: finding unit rates (cost per item or units per minute) to compare different-sized deals, choose the better buy, and compute total cost
cert: solving better-buy and rate problems using unit rates

intro.caption: Lesson 3-8 — solving problems with unit rates. Drift Crew needs grip pads, boost cells, and coolant before race day. Each supplier packs a different amount, so total price alone can fool you!

balloons.t: Live from the Parts Shop! The 4-pack is $10 and the 10-pack is $21. Ten bucks wins!
Hold on, Omar. Different pack sizes! Find the cost per ONE pad first.
Ten dollars is less than twenty-one dollars! Even my lunch sandwich knows that!
Sure, if you only want 4 pads. Divide cost by quantity to see what ONE pad costs!

pages.caption: A lower total price does not mean a better buy when the pack sizes differ. Compare the unit rate (cost per 1 item).

balloons.t: Unit price = total cost ÷ number of items. Let's price ONE pad in each pack.
Careful! The biggest pack is not always the cheapest per unit. Always divide!
Compare the unit prices side by side. Lower cost per item is the better buy.
Once we know the unit price, we multiply by how many parts our kart needs.
Wait—for charging speed, a HIGHER rate per minute wins! Context matters!
Three final orders at the register. Find the unit rate, compare, and ring up the total!
New grip pads, full boost, and money left in the pit budget. Smart shopping!

win.caption: Unit rates let you compare deals fairly across different pack sizes. Divide total cost by quantity for unit price, then multiply by the amount you need.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Find the Unit Price
gates.prompt: Find the unit price (cost for 1 grip pad) for both packs.
hints: Conceptual: unit price tells you what ONE item costs, so you can compare different pack sizes fairly.
Procedural: divide the total price by the number of pads: price ÷ quantity.

steps: The unit price is $1.50 per bolt.
worked.q: What is the unit price if 5 bolts cost $10.00?

items.label: 4 grip pads for $10.00 → $___ per pad
items.aria: unit price of 4 grip pads for 10 dollars

fb.msg: 0.4 is 4 ÷ 10 (pads per dollar). For dollars per pad, divide $10 by 4.
That multiplied 10 × 4. Divide the total price by the number of pads.

items.label: 10 grip pads for $21.00 → $___ per pad
items.aria: unit price of 10 grip pads for 21 dollars

fb.msg: Divide $21 by 10 pads instead of multiplying.
That subtracted 10 from 21. Divide cost by quantity.

gates.pass: The 4-pack is $2.50 per pad, while the 10-pack is $2.10 per pad! Omar quietly puts the 4-pack back.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Pick the Better Buy
gates.prompt: Compare two boost-cell deals. Remember: the biggest pack is not always the best deal!
hints: Conceptual: the better buy is the deal with the LOWER cost per single item, not the lower total or bigger box.
Procedural: compute price ÷ quantity for each option, then pick the smaller unit price.

steps: Practice: 6 fuses for $9.00 vs 10 fuses for $18.00.
10-pack: $18.00 ÷ 10 = $1.80 each. The 6-pack is the better buy!
worked.q: Which is the better buy: 3 tires for $24 or 5 tires for $45?

items.q:
Deal A: 6 boost cells for $18.00.
Deal B: 12 boost cells for $42.00.
Which is the better buy?

options.fb: Deal B has a bigger box, but $3.50 per cell costs more than $3.00 per cell.

options.t: They cost the same per cell

options.fb: Both deals give total cost and quantity, so you can divide to compare unit prices.

items.label: How much cheaper PER CELL is Deal A than Deal B? $___
items.aria: difference in unit price between Deal A and Deal B

fb.msg: 24 is the difference in total price ($42 − $18), not the difference per cell.
$3.00 is Deal A's unit price. Subtract $3.00 from Deal B's $3.50.

items.fbDefault: Subtract Deal A's unit price ($3.00) from Deal B's unit price ($3.50).

gates.pass: Deal A wins at $3.00 per cell—saving $0.50 on every single boost cell!

gates.title: Gate 3 · Fill the Team Cart
gates.prompt: Find the cost for a full team order, and check a charging rate where HIGHER is better.
hints: Conceptual: for prices, lower per unit is better; for speed or output per minute, higher per unit is faster.
Procedural: find the unit rate first (divide), then multiply by the number of items needed.

steps: Practice: 4 coolant cans cost $14.00. How much do 10 cans cost?
worked.q: If 2 cans cost $7.00, how much do 6 cans cost?

items.label: Coolant sells at 5 cans for $16.00. How much do 15 cans cost? $___

fb.msg: $3.20 is the cost for ONE can. Multiply by 15 cans for the team order.
That's 10 cans ($3.20 × 10). The team needs 15 cans.

items.fbDefault: Find the unit price ($16 ÷ 5 = $3.20), then multiply by 15.

items.q: Charger X pumps 120 boost units in 4 minutes. Charger Y pumps 175 in 5 minutes. Which charger is faster?

options.fb: For charging speed, you want MORE units per minute, not fewer. 35 > 30.

options.t: Both charge at the same rate
Charger X because 4 minutes is shorter
options.fb: 4 minutes is shorter, but it also pumped fewer units. Compare units per 1 minute.

gates.pass: 15 cans for $48, and Charger Y pumps 35 units per minute! Cart loaded!

gates.title: Boss Gate · Checkout Showdown
gates.prompt: Clear all three register checks to equip the Drift Crew for race day.
hints: Conceptual: never compare raw totals when quantities differ. Always find the rate for 1 unit first.
Procedural: unit price = cost ÷ quantity; total cost = unit price × needed quantity.

steps: Practice: 5 decals cost $6.50, and 10 decals cost $11.00.
Better buy is $1.10 each. For 15 decals: 15 × $1.10 = $16.50.
worked.q: If 1 decal costs $1.10, how much do 15 decals cost?

items.q: Lock 1 · 8 wing bolts for $12.00 or 12 wing bolts for $16.80. Which is the better buy?

options.fb: $1.50 per bolt is higher than $1.40 per bolt.

options.t: They have the same unit price

items.label: Lock 2 · At $1.40 per bolt, how much do 20 bolts cost? $___

fb.msg: 14 is 10 bolts ($1.40 × 10). Double it for 20 bolts.

items.label: Lock 3 · A pit drone delivers 180 parts in 6 trips. How many parts per trip?

fb.msg: Divide 180 parts by 6 trips instead of multiplying.

gates.pass: CA-CHING! Every part priced, compared, and loaded under budget!

journal.heading: Lesson 3-8 — what the parts showdown taught us
rows: Divide total cost by quantity (cost ÷ items) to find the price of ONE item.
Compare unit prices, not total prices or box sizes. The lower cost per unit is the better buy.
Multiply the unit price by the number of items you need to get your total cost.
Lower is better for price per item, while higher is better for speed or output per minute.
journal.quote: "A smaller price tag only wins if you ignore how many parts are in the box." — Lin

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 3-8 (Solve Problems with Unit Rates). Covers calculating unit prices, comparing better buys across different package sizes, scaling unit rates to a target quantity, and comparing output rates.
standards: Understand and use unit rates to solve real-world problems and compare deals
